title: Life cycle close
hook: a life, from the adhan in the ear to the prayer without an adhan

segments.voice: Yesterday, inheritance: the shares the Qur'an names, with something and a kind word for those present. Today, the whole road at once.

A baby, a few hours old, in someone's arms. A parent or a grandparent leans in close to the tiny right ear and says the adhan, softly: Allahu akbar. Some families do this, and it's where this stretch of the path began. Now the other end of the road: a funeral. People stand in rows behind the imam for the funeral prayer, and before it, no adhan is called at all. Some people put those two moments side by side and say a life is the space between the call and the prayer. That's a saying people tell, not a verse. But it makes a good map.
screen: `THE CALL IN A NEWBORN'S EAR.` → `A PRAYER WITH NO CALL.` → `A LIFE IN BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: Walk the road again, and watch whose hands do the work. At the start, someone else says the call in your ear, touches a softened date to your mouth, chooses your name, shares the meat of the sacrifice, shaves your hair and gives its weight in silver. You're carried. Then the middle, and the hands become yours. Learning to pray. Finishing the Qur'an, the khatm. Coming of age, when the duties begin. Choosing a spouse, giving consent, the nikah, a home where, as surah al-Rum puts it, two people may dwell in tranquility. Serving a family, shepherding a flock, honoring the elders who once carried you. Then the road bends: visiting the sick, remembering death. And at the end, the hands go back to the community. Someone washes you, wraps you in plain white cloth, stands in rows to pray over you, lays you facing the qiblah, cooks for your family, writes the shares of what you left. The Qur'an says it plainly in surah Al 'Imran, in Pickthall's words: "Every soul will taste of death." And surah al-Baqarah describes the patient, who say when misfortune strikes: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." So the shape of a Muslim life, as these customs draw it, is carried, then carrying, then carried again. The middle is the part a person lives with their own hands, and that's where the path goes next: the festival year.
screen: `SOMEONE ELSE SAYS YOUR CALL.` · `THE MIDDLE IS YOURS TO LIVE.` · `SOMEONE ELSE SAYS YOUR PRAYER.` · `CARRIED, CARRYING, CARRIED AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Ask, without hurrying: where am I on the road right now, being carried, carrying someone, or somewhere in between? Notice who carried you to get here, and who you're carrying now, even in a small way, without judging the stage. If you pray, you can remember the people at both ends of your road.
Life cycle close. The whole road, from the adhan in a newborn's ear to the funeral prayer that has no adhan, with the community's hands at both ends. Today's word.
Your line: from call to prayer. The middle is yours to live. Tomorrow, the sacred months.

howItsDone: Some Muslim families say the adhan softly in a newborn's ear, and at the end of life the community washes, shrouds and prays over the body in a funeral prayer that has no adhan; on hearing of a death, the words of Qur'an 2:156 are said: "we are Allah's and unto Him we are returning."

chat.says: What does a newborn's first call to prayer have to do with a funeral?
options: Some say a life is the gap between that call and the funeral prayer, which has none.
Nothing; the funeral prayer is always opened with its own full adhan, like any other.
The same person must say both, so the whole life is blessed by one voice.
chat.meaning: No adhan is called before the funeral prayer. Some people say a life is the space between the call in a newborn's ear and that prayer.

notes: Confirm the statement that no adhan or iqamah is called for the funeral prayer (the standard position across the schools).
The saying that a life is the space between the adhan at birth and the funeral prayer is presented as a saying people tell, not a source. Confirm the framing.
Abu Dawud 5105 on the adhan in the newborn's ear is graded weak by some hadith scholars; the script says only that some families do this.
The teach recaps the block's days (date, naming, sacrifice, hair, prayer, khatm, nikah, etc.) without numbers; confirm the recap matches the earlier scripts.
Confirm Pickthall's exact wording of 3:185 (first sentence) and 2:156.
